why: Every sales team lives by its pipeline and its forecast. Account executives and key account managers are judged on how well they run their deals, predict their number and grow their accounts, and interviews test exactly that: stages, metrics, coverage, quota maths and account plans.
outcome: define pipeline stages with buyer-based exit criteria, keep a CRM a manager can trust, compute win rate, sales velocity, weighted pipeline, coverage and quota attainment, build an honest forecast, plan a territory from the quota, write a key account plan and protect renewals with net revenue retention in mind.

lessons.title: Pipeline stages with exit criteria
text: A sales pipeline is the list of open opportunities, each sitting in a stage that says how far the buyer has gone. The stages are not decoration: the forecast, the coverage ratio and the conversion rates in this course all come from them. If two reps put the same deal in different stages, every number built on the pipeline is wrong.

Each stage needs an exit criterion: the verifiable event that moves a deal to the next stage. The best criteria are things the buyer did, not things the seller did. “Proposal sent” is a seller action; it says nothing about the buyer’s intent. “The buyer confirmed the budget and agreed a decision date” is a buyer action you can check. A deal moves forward when the buyer moves, not when the rep is busy.

Stages should mirror how the customer buys: they recognise a problem, explore options, choose a solution, get approval and sign. A typical B2B pipeline has five to seven open stages (qualification, discovery, solution or demo, proposal, negotiation), then closed won or closed lost. Each stage carries a default stage probability (for example 10 % at qualification, 60 % at proposal) used by the weighted pipeline. Those percentages should come from the team’s own history, not from a template, and be reviewed once or twice a year.

Qualification frameworks fit naturally into the exit criteria. BANT (budget, authority, need, timeline) is the classic quick check; MEDDIC and MEDDPICC (metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, paper process, identify pain, champion, competition) are used for complex deals. A company might require, for example, an identified pain and a champion to leave discovery, and a meeting with the economic buyer before the proposal stage.

In real jobs, the classic problems are happy ears (moving a deal forward because the meeting felt good), skipped stages (a deal jumps from discovery to negotiation and nobody knows who signs) and deals that never move backwards. If the champion leaves or the budget is frozen, move the deal back or close it as lost: an honest pipeline is smaller, but it is usable.
points: A stage describes what the buyer has done, checked by an exit criterion.
Stages follow the customer’s buying process: typically 5 to 7 open stages, then closed won or closed lost.
Each stage has a default stage probability taken from the team’s own history.
BANT and MEDDIC / MEDDPICC items make good exit criteria.
Deals can move backwards: a stage reached once is not kept forever.

example.code:
Stage          Exit criterion (what the buyer did)                  Probability
1 Qualify      Agreed to a discovery call; pain confirmed             10%
2 Discovery    Shared the problem, its impact and decision process    20%
3 Solution     Saw a tailored demo; named the economic buyer          40%
4 Proposal     Received pricing; agreed a decision date               60%
5 Negotiation  Verbal yes; legal and procurement engaged              80%
6 Closed won   Signed the order form                                 100%
example.note: Every exit criterion is something you can verify with the buyer: an e-mail, a meeting, a signed document. The probabilities are an example; use your team’s history.

lessons.title: CRM hygiene
text: The CRM (Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Microsoft Dynamics…) is the single record of every account, contact and opportunity. In Salesforce, a lead is a person not yet qualified; once qualified it is converted into an account (the company), a contact (the person) and an opportunity (the deal), and the opportunity carries the stage, the amount and the close date. HubSpot uses companies, contacts and deals, with deal stages inside one or more pipelines. The names change; the logic is the same.

Good hygiene comes down to a few fields on every open opportunity: an amount that reflects the latest pricing discussion, a close date that is the buyer’s decision date (not the end of the quarter you hope for), the stage according to the exit criteria, the contacts involved with their role, and a next step with a date. “Follow up” is not a next step; “Demo for the IT director on 14 March, invitation accepted” is.

Managers look for two warning signs. A stale deal has had no activity logged for a while (30 days is a common threshold, it varies by company and cycle). A slipped deal has had its close date pushed out, often again and again. A deal whose close date moved three times is rarely about to close: it needs a real conversation with the buyer, or closing as lost.

Why managers care: the forecast, the team’s targets and often the company’s hiring and spending plans are built on the CRM. A sales manager reports a number to their director every week, and that number is the sum of what the reps typed. Missing fields also hide patterns that could help you, such as which lead source converts best or at which stage deals die.

Make it a routine, not a punishment: log calls and meetings the same day (most CRMs sync e-mail and calendar), update the next step at the end of every customer meeting, and spend fifteen minutes before your weekly pipeline review closing or updating everything that is out of date. Record what the buyer said, not what you hope.
points: Every open deal: amount, realistic close date, stage, contacts with roles, next step with a date.
The close date is when the buyer decides, not the end of your quarter.
Stale deals (no recent activity) and slipped deals (close date pushed again) are warning signs.
The forecast is only as good as the CRM data behind it.

example.code:
BAD
Opportunity: Dupont Logistics - new deal
Stage: Proposal      Amount: 50,000      Close date: 31/12
Next step: follow up

GOOD
Opportunity: Dupont Logistics - fleet tracking, 3 sites
Stage: Proposal (pricing sent 04/03, decision date agreed: 28/03)
Amount: 42,000 (3 sites x 14,000; 8% discount discussed, not agreed)
Contacts: ops director (champion); CFO (economic buyer, not met yet)
Next step: 12/03 call with CFO + ops director to review the business case (invite accepted)
example.note: The good record lets a manager understand the deal in twenty seconds, and it shows the gap honestly: the economic buyer has not been met yet.

lessons.title: Funnel metrics
text: Funnel metrics turn the pipeline into a model of how your sales work. The stage conversion rate is the share of deals that move from one stage to the next: 120 discovery calls and 54 demos is a 45 % conversion. It shows where deals die: if many demos never become proposals, the problem is the demo or the qualification before it.

Win rate is the share of closed deals that were won: won / (won + lost). Open deals are left out, because they are not decided yet. Say whether you count deals or value (a few large wins can make the value win rate look very different) and from which stage you count: the win rate from the first meeting is much lower than the win rate from the proposal stage. Compare like with like.

Average deal size is the total value of won deals divided by their number, and sales cycle length is the average number of days from opportunity creation to closed won. Both vary by segment: a mid-market deal may close in 45 days while a large account takes nine months, so look at them per segment rather than as one blended figure.

Sales velocity combines the four levers into one number: velocity = (number of opportunities × win rate × average deal size) / sales cycle length in days. With 40 opportunities, a 25 % win rate, an average deal of 18,000 € and a 60-day cycle, the pipeline produces 40 × 0.25 × 18,000 / 60 = 3,000 € of revenue per day. Improving any lever raises velocity; shortening the cycle is often the least obvious one.

In interviews, expect to compute these on the spot and to say which lever you would work on first. A good answer is specific: “my demo-to-proposal conversion was 30 % against 50 % for the team, so I started sending a written recap of the buyer’s pains after each demo”. Numbers without a diagnosis and an action are only half an answer.
points: Stage conversion rate = deals reaching the next stage / deals in this stage.
Win rate = won / (won + lost); open deals are excluded.
Average deal size and sales cycle length: per segment, not blended.
Sales velocity = opportunities × win rate × average deal size / cycle length (days).

example.code:
A                    B
1    Opportunities        40
2    Win rate             0.25
3    Average deal size    18000
4    Cycle (days)         60
5    Velocity per day     =B1*B2*B3/B4      -> 3000
example.note: Each of the four inputs is a lever: more opportunities, a better win rate, bigger deals or a shorter cycle all raise the revenue per day.

lessons.title: Coverage and the forecast
text: The weighted pipeline multiplies each open deal by its stage probability and adds them up: in Excel, =SUMPRODUCT(amounts, probabilities). Five deals worth 170,000 € in total weigh only 62,000 € in the example below. It is a useful view of a whole pipeline, especially for a large team where averages even out, but a poor forecast for one rep with a few deals: a deal is won or lost, never won at 40 %.

That is why most teams also use forecast categories, a judgement the rep makes deal by deal. Salesforce’s default set: Pipeline (open, still early or uncertain for this period), Best case (could close this period if things go well), Commit (the rep is confident it will close this period and will be held to it), Closed (won) and Omitted (left out of the forecast). The number a manager hears is usually closed + commit, with best case as the upside.

Pipeline coverage compares the open pipeline for the period with what is still needed: coverage = open pipeline / (target − already closed). With a 500,000 € quarterly target, 180,000 € closed and 960,000 € of open pipeline due this quarter, coverage is 960,000 / 320,000 = 3×. The well-known 3× rule of thumb assumes roughly a one-in-three win rate on that pipeline; the coverage you need is about 1 / win rate, so a team that wins 25 % needs about 4×.

Forecast accuracy measures how close the forecast was to the result, for example forecast error = (actual − forecast) / forecast. A rep who calls 200,000 € and closes 150,000 € missed by 25 %. One who calls 100,000 € and closes 180,000 € was probably sandbagging, which also hurts the company, because it plans hiring and cash on the forecast. Managers trust a reliable commit more than a big but random number.

Coverage can mislead: a pipeline full of stale deals, inflated amounts or close dates pushed into the quarter makes 3× look safe when it is not. Check quality as well as quantity: how much of the pipeline has met the economic buyer, has a next step this week, and has never slipped?
points: Weighted pipeline = SUMPRODUCT(amount, stage probability).
Forecast categories: pipeline, best case, commit, closed (and omitted).
Pipeline coverage = open pipeline / (target − closed); coverage needed ≈ 1 / win rate.
Forecast accuracy matters as much as the size of the number: no happy ears, no sandbagging.

example.code:
A          B          C
1    Deal       Amount     Probability
2    Atlas      40000      0.2
3    Borealis   25000      0.6
4    Cobalt     60000      0.4
5    Delta      15000      0.8
6    Eiffel     30000      0.1
7    Total      =SUM(B2:B6)                  -> 170000
8    Weighted   =SUMPRODUCT(B2:B6,C2:C6)     -> 62000
example.note: 170,000 € of pipeline, but only 62,000 € once weighted. Against a remaining target of 60,000 € the weighted view looks fine; whether it is depends on which of these deals the rep would really commit.

lessons.title: Quota, territory and account planning
text: A quota is the sales target a rep is measured against, usually yearly and split by quarter, in bookings, new ARR or margin depending on the company. Quota attainment = closed won / quota: 165,000 € closed against a 150,000 € quarterly quota is 110 %. Variable pay (a commission plan, often with accelerators above 100 %) is linked to it, so read your compensation plan carefully: what counts, when, and with which caps.

Work backwards from the quota to the activity it needs. A 600,000 € annual quota with an average deal of 20,000 € means 30 deals. With a 25 % win rate on opportunities, that is 120 opportunities. If 40 % of first meetings become qualified opportunities, 300 first meetings. Over about 46 working weeks, that is 6 to 7 first meetings a week, and if one prospect in ten accepts a meeting, roughly 65 new prospects contacted every week. These are averages, not guarantees, but they turn a scary number into a weekly plan.

A territory is the set of accounts a rep may sell to: a region (Île-de-France, DACH), an industry (retail, healthcare), a size band (companies of 200 to 1,000 employees) or a list of named accounts. Good territory design gives each rep a fair potential and avoids two reps chasing the same company. Rules of engagement say who owns an account when a contact moves or a subsidiary buys.

Inside a territory, tier the accounts so your time follows the potential. A common approach: tier A (best fit with the ideal customer profile, ICP, and high potential: researched one by one, several contacts approached), tier B (good fit: semi-personalised sequences), tier C (low potential or weak fit: automated or marketing-led). Fit can be scored on industry, size, tools already used, growth signals and existing relationships.

Hiring managers often ask how you would approach your first 90 days in a territory. A strong answer: learn the product and the ICP, review the existing pipeline and accounts, tier the territory, build the activity plan from the quota as above, and agree the first checkpoints with your manager.
points: Quota attainment = closed won / quota.
Quota → deals (÷ average deal size) → opportunities (÷ win rate) → meetings → prospects.
Territory: region, industry, size or named accounts, with clear rules of engagement.
Account tiering (A / B / C) on ICP fit and potential; most of your time goes to tier A.

example.code:
A                        B
1    Annual quota             600000
2    Average deal size        20000
3    Win rate                 0.25
4    Meeting to opportunity   0.4
5    Working weeks            46
6    Deals needed             =B1/B2      -> 30
7    Opportunities needed     =B6/B3      -> 120
8    First meetings needed    =B7/B4      -> 300
9    Meetings per week        =B8/B5      -> 6.5
example.note: Each line divides by one conversion rate. Change one assumption (a 30 % win rate, a bigger average deal) and the weekly effort changes with it.

lessons.title: Key account management
text: Key account managers look after a few large customers that matter most for revenue and growth. The job is less about new logos and more about growing and protecting existing relationships: renewals, new departments, new countries, new products. In a strategic account model, one person coordinates sales, customer success, support and executives for each key account.

The account plan is the working document for one key account, updated every quarter. Typical sections: the customer’s business and strategy (annual report, press, conversations), their goals and challenges this year, our current footprint (products, sites, revenue, contract dates), the relationship map, the whitespace, our objectives for the account with numbers, the action plan with owners and dates, and the risks.

The relationship map lists the people who matter in the buying decision and how they see you: the economic buyer (who signs or controls the budget), the champion (who sells for you internally and has influence), coaches (who give you information), users, and blockers. Being single-threaded, with one contact only, is the biggest account risk: if that person leaves, the account is exposed. Build several relationships at several levels.

Whitespace is the business you could do but do not do yet: products the customer has not bought, sites, subsidiaries or departments not yet covered. A simple grid of business units (rows) against products (columns), each cell marked customer, opportunity, competitor or not relevant, shows where to grow and where a competitor sits.

A QBR (quarterly business review) is the regular meeting with the customer’s sponsors: what was achieved against their goals, usage and results, issues and how they were fixed, the plan for next quarter. A good QBR is about their business, not a sales pitch, and it earns the right to discuss the next project. Prepare it with numbers and send a written summary afterwards.
points: Account plan: business, goals, footprint, relationship map, whitespace, objectives, actions, risks.
Relationship map: economic buyer, champion, coaches, users, blockers.
Single-threaded (one contact) is the biggest risk: build relationships at several levels.
Whitespace grid: business units × products.
QBR: value delivered against the customer’s goals, then the next steps.

example.code:
RELATIONSHIP MAP - Nordia Retail (key account)
Name / role                 Influence  Attitude   Our contact
CFO (economic buyer)        High       Neutral    Met once, at the Q2 QBR
Head of supply chain        High       Champion   Monthly call
IT director                 Medium     Sceptical  Only through the champion  <- risk
Store operations managers   Low        Positive   Users, trained

WHITESPACE          Tracking     Analytics     Support plus
France              Customer     Customer      Opportunity
Belgium             Customer     Opportunity   -
Spain (acquired)    Competitor   Opportunity   -
example.note: The map shows the risk at a glance (the IT director is reached only through the champion), and the grid shows two growth paths: analytics in Belgium and Spain, and the Spanish sites held by a competitor.

lessons.title: Renewals, upsell, cross-sell and churn
text: In subscription businesses (SaaS, service contracts, maintenance), much of each year’s revenue comes from existing customers. Churn is the revenue lost when customers leave or do not renew; contraction is the revenue lost when they stay but buy less (fewer licences, a cheaper plan). Expansion is the revenue added from existing customers: upsell (more of the same product or a higher tier) and cross-sell (another product).

Net revenue retention (NRR) sums it up: NRR = (starting ARR + expansion − contraction − churn) / starting ARR, over a period (usually 12 months) and for the customers you had at the start. With 1,000,000 € of starting ARR, 180,000 € of expansion, 40,000 € of contraction and 60,000 € of churn, NRR = 1,080,000 / 1,000,000 = 108 %: the existing base grew even without new customers. Gross revenue retention (GRR) leaves expansion out: 900,000 / 1,000,000 = 90 %, and it can never exceed 100 %.

The customer success handoff from sales decides a lot of the renewal. Pass on what was promised, the customer’s success criteria and metrics, the stakeholders and their roles, the timeline and the risks. A customer who was oversold during the sales cycle churns a year later; managers and investors watch NRR precisely because it shows whether the sales were good sales.

Watch the early warning signs: usage dropping, the champion leaving, a new executive or a merger, more support tickets or escalations, late payments, nobody attending the QBR, a question about the contract’s termination terms. Start renewal conversations early, often 90 to 120 days before the end date for large contracts, so there is time to fix a problem.

Upsell and cross-sell work when they follow value: the customer reached the goal of the first project, so the next department or the next module is a logical step. Pushing a bigger deal into an unhappy account damages trust and the renewal. Interviewers like candidates who know their NRR or renewal rate and can explain one account they saved and one they expanded.
points: Churn = revenue lost from customers who leave; contraction = they stay but pay less.
Upsell = more of the same product or a higher tier; cross-sell = another product.
NRR = (start + expansion − contraction − churn) / start; GRR leaves out expansion (100 % at most).
Customer success handoff: promises, success criteria, stakeholders, risks.
Early warning signs: usage down, champion gone, tickets up, nobody at the QBR.

example.code:
A                  B
1    Starting ARR       1000000
2    Expansion          180000
3    Contraction        40000
4    Churn              60000
5    NRR                =(B1+B2-B3-B4)/B1     -> 1.08
6    GRR                =(B1-B3-B4)/B1        -> 0.9
example.note: NRR above 100 % means the existing customers alone grow the revenue. GRR shows the leak before expansion hides it.

lessons.title: Running your week and talking to your manager
text: A rep’s week usually has a fixed rhythm: protected prospecting blocks (many teams keep mornings for calls), customer meetings, follow-ups and proposals, and internal meetings: a weekly one-to-one, a team pipeline review and, near the end of the quarter, forecast calls. Plan the week from your numbers: how many first meetings you need (lesson 5), which deals lack a next step, which renewals are coming.

Three internal meetings, three purposes. The pipeline review looks at the whole pipeline: is there enough, at the right stages, with clean data? The deal review goes deep into one important deal: what do we know, what is missing, what is the plan? The forecast call agrees the number for the period: what is commit, what is best case, what changed since last week.

Expect deal review questions built on MEDDPICC. Metrics: what measurable gain does the customer expect? Economic buyer: who is it and have we met them? Decision criteria and decision process: how will they choose, and what are the steps to signature, including the paper process (legal, procurement, security review)? Identify pain: what problem are they solving and what happens if they do nothing? Champion: who sells for us and how have we tested them? Competition: who else, including doing nothing or building in-house? “I don’t know yet, I will ask on Thursday’s call” is a fine answer; guessing is not.

Report honestly. Bad news early is a gift to your manager: they can bring an executive, a pre-sales engineer or a pricing exception while there is still time. Two habits destroy trust: happy ears (calling a deal commit because the buyer was friendly) and sandbagging (hiding a deal you expect to win to look good later or to protect next quarter). Both make the forecast useless.

Come to your one-to-one prepared: your numbers against target, your three biggest deals with their next steps and risks, where you need help, and one thing you learnt. Short, factual and ending with a clear request: that is the format managers remember.
points: Pipeline review = the whole pipeline; deal review = one deal in depth; forecast call = the number.
MEDDPICC questions show what is known and what is missing in a deal.
Bad news early, with a plan; no happy ears, no sandbagging.
One-to-one: numbers, top deals, risks, the help you need.

example.code:
DEAL REVIEW - Helios Energy, 120,000 / year, stage: Proposal, close date 30/06
Metrics:           cut field-visit planning time by 30% (their estimate, workshop 12/05)
Economic buyer:    COO - NOT MET YET (meeting requested through the champion)
Decision criteria: SAP integration, hosting in France, price per site
Decision process:  ops team -> COO -> procurement -> signature
Paper process:     their contract template; legal review ~3 weeks; security review 2 weeks
Identify pain:     planning on spreadsheets, 2 contracts lost last year because of delays
Champion:          head of field operations - tested: shared the budget figure
Competition:       one other vendor + build in-house
Ask:               manager to join the COO meeting; pricing approval for a 3-year term
Risk:              30/06 not realistic if legal takes 3 weeks -> best case, not commit
example.note: A one-page deal review: facts, gaps in capitals, a clear request to the manager and an honest call on the forecast category.

items: Verifiable buyer action that moves a deal to the next stage
Default chance of winning at a stage, from the team’s history
A dated action agreed with the buyer
When the buyer decides, not the end of your quarter
No activity logged for a long time (e.g. 30 days)
Close date pushed out, often more than once
Deals reaching the next stage / deals in this stage
Value of won deals / number of won deals
Average days from opportunity creation to closed won
Opportunities × win rate × average deal size / cycle days
Rep is confident it closes this period and is held to it
Could close this period if things go well: the upside
Open but early or uncertain for this period
Open pipeline / (target − closed); need ≈ 1 / win rate
How close the forecast was: (actual − forecast) / forecast
The sales target a rep is measured against
The accounts a rep may sell to: region, industry, size or named list
A / B / C by ICP fit and potential
Ideal customer profile: the companies that fit best
Goals, footprint, relationship map, whitespace, actions, risks
Who decides, who supports, who blocks
Products, sites or units not yet sold
Quarterly business review with the customer’s sponsors
More or a higher tier of the same product / another product
Metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, paper process, identify pain, champion, competition
Who signs or controls the budget
Insider with influence who sells for you
Hearing a yes that the buyer never gave
Hiding deals you expect to win to look good later

pitfalls: Defining stages by what the seller did (“proposal sent”) instead of what the buyer did.
Leaving close dates at the end of the quarter and pushing them again and again without talking to the buyer.
Counting open deals in the win rate, or comparing win rates measured from different stages.
Treating the weighted pipeline as a promise for one rep with a few large deals.
Relying on 3× coverage without checking your own win rate and the quality of the pipeline.
Being single-threaded on a key account: one contact leaves and the renewal is at risk.
Happy ears and sandbagging: both make the forecast useless and cost your manager’s trust.

exercises.q: Put these pipeline stages in order, from first contact to signature.
steps: Qualification: the prospect agreed to a discovery call
Discovery: the buyer shared the problem, its impact and the decision process
Solution: the buyer saw a tailored demo and named the economic buyer
Proposal: the buyer received pricing and agreed a decision date
Negotiation: verbal yes, legal and procurement engaged
Closed won: the order form is signed
exercises.answer: The stages follow the buyer’s journey: problem, options, choice, approval, signature. Each one ends with something the buyer did.

exercises.q: Sort these candidate exit criteria: buyer actions (good criteria) or seller actions (poor criteria).

groups.name: Buyer action
items: The buyer confirmed the budget range
The economic buyer attended the demo
The prospect agreed a decision date

groups.name: Seller action
items: We connected with the contact on LinkedIn

exercises.answer: A stage should move when the buyer moves. Seller actions show effort, not progress: you can send ten proposals to a prospect who will never buy.

exercises.q: Match each forecast category with its definition.
pairs: The rep is confident it closes this period and will be held to it
Could close this period if things go well: the upside
Open, but early or uncertain for this period
Left out of the forecast (lost, out of scope)
exercises.answer: The number a manager reports is usually closed + commit, with best case as the upside. These are Salesforce’s default categories; some companies rename them.

exercises.q: In E2, Lea’s win rate (closed deals only).
exercises.hint: Win rate = won / (won + lost). Open deals are not decided yet.
exercises.explain: 12 / (12 + 28) = 0.30, a 30 % win rate. Dividing by B2+C2+D2 would count the 15 open deals as losses and give 22 %, which understates the result.

exercises.q: In B7, the weighted pipeline (each amount × its probability, added up).
exercises.hint: Use SUMPRODUCT on the amount column and the probability column.

exercises.q: In D2, the pipeline coverage for the rest of the quarter.
exercises.explain: 800,000 / (400,000 − 150,000) = 800,000 / 250,000 = 3.2×. Dividing by the full target (2×) ignores what is already won and makes the quarter look riskier than it is.

exercises.q: In E2, the sales velocity per day.
exercises.hint: Velocity = opportunities × win rate × average deal size / cycle length in days.
exercises.explain: 60 × 0.2 × 15,000 / 90 = 180,000 / 90 = 2,000 € of revenue per day. Shortening the cycle to 60 days would raise it to 3,000 € a day.

exercises.q: In D3, Hugo’s quota attainment for the quarter.
In D2, how many more deals are needed to reach the quota? Round up to a whole deal.
exercises.hint: (Quota − closed so far) / average deal size, rounded up with ROUNDUP(…, 0).
exercises.explain: (600,000 − 250,000) / 20,000 = 17.5, so 18 deals: half a deal does not exist. At a 25 % win rate, that means about 72 more opportunities.

exercises.q: In E2, the net revenue retention (NRR) of the year.
exercises.hint: NRR = (starting ARR + expansion − contraction − churn) / starting ARR.

exercises.q: Your team wins about 25 % of its open pipeline. Roughly how many times the remaining target should the open pipeline be? Answer with a number.
exercises.answer: Coverage needed ≈ 1 / win rate = 1 / 0.25 = 4×. The 3× rule of thumb only works for a team that wins about one deal in three.

exercises.q: Three weeks before quarter-end, your biggest deal (Helios, 120,000 €, 40 % of your remaining target) is in commit. Since the proposal the champion answers slowly, the economic buyer has not been met and legal has not received the contract. It comes up in the pipeline review.

steps.text: Your manager asks: “Is Helios still commit?”

choices.label: Yes: the champion told me it is a priority
choices.feedback: Happy ears. A friendly champion is not a signature: without the economic buyer and the contract at legal, the deal cannot be called commit.

choices.label: Give the facts: no economic buyer meeting, contract not at legal, so best case until those happen
choices.feedback: Honest and specific. Your manager can now help while there is still time, and the forecast stays reliable.

choices.label: Quietly take it out of the forecast to avoid questions
choices.feedback: Hiding a deal is sandbagging: the manager loses the chance to help and the forecast is wrong in the other direction.

steps.text: What do you do this week?

choices.label: Ask the champion for a meeting with the COO and build a mutual close plan with dates up to signature
choices.feedback: This tests the deal: a real buyer agrees to the steps and dates; a deal that will not close shows it now.

choices.label: Offer 15 % off if they sign before quarter-end
choices.feedback: An unrequested discount costs margin, teaches the buyer to wait for the quarter-end and does not fix the missing economic buyer.

choices.label: Wait: chasing too much looks desperate
choices.feedback: Three weeks is short when legal alone may take that long. Waiting turns a risk into a surprise.

steps.text: The champion admits the COO wants to compare one more vendor; signature will be in August at best.

choices.label: Move the close date to August, take it out of this quarter’s commit, tell your manager and look for other deals to close the gap
choices.feedback: The CRM now matches reality, the manager can adjust the forecast, and you still have three weeks to work on other deals.

choices.label: Keep 30 June in the CRM until the last day, just in case
choices.feedback: A slipped deal discovered on the last day leaves no time to react, and your next commit will be doubted.

exercises.answer: Call the deal on facts, test it with a mutual close plan and the economic buyer, and update the forecast as soon as the facts change. Bad news early is useful; bad news late is a surprise.

exercises.q: Nordia Retail is one of your key accounts: a chain of 120 stores in France and Belgium that has used your stock-tracking software in France for two years (180,000 € ARR, renewal in nine months). It has just acquired a chain in Spain that uses a competitor. Your only regular contact is the head of supply chain. Write the outline of your account plan: the sections and what you would put in each.
exercises.answer: 1) Account overview: Nordia’s business, strategy and recent news (the Spanish acquisition), key figures. 2) Customer goals this year: for example lower stock-outs, integrate the Spanish stores, cut costs; ask them, do not guess. 3) Our footprint: tracking in France, 180,000 € ARR, contract end date, usage and results so far (the value proof for the renewal). 4) Relationship map: head of supply chain (champion), CFO (economic buyer), IT director, store operations, Spanish management; gaps: single-threaded, no relationship with the CFO or in Spain. 5) Whitespace: tracking in Belgium, analytics module, Spanish stores (competitor in place: contract end date, satisfaction). 6) Objectives with numbers: renew at 180,000 € or more nine months from now, one expansion (for example Belgium) this year, meet the CFO and the Spanish team this quarter. 7) Action plan with owners and dates: QBR with the CFO in the next 60 days on the results delivered, executive sponsor from our side, discovery with the Spanish team, start renewal talks at least 90 days before the end date. 8) Risks and mitigation: champion leaves, the Spanish tool is chosen for the whole group, budget freeze after the acquisition.

interview.q: How do you manage your pipeline?
interview.a: I use stages with buyer-based exit criteria, so a deal only moves when the buyer does something I can verify. Every deal has an amount, a close date agreed with the buyer and a dated next step. Each week I update the CRM before the pipeline review, close what is dead and check my coverage against what I still need. I also watch my conversion by stage to see where I lose deals and work on that stage.

interview.q: How do you build your forecast, and how accurate was it?
interview.a: Deal by deal: commit only when the economic buyer is engaged, the decision process and paper process are known and the close date is confirmed by the buyer; best case for deals that could close with one more step. I check it against the weighted pipeline and my historical win rate. Then give a real figure, for example: last year my commit landed within 10 % of the result in three quarters out of four, and when I missed I said so early.

interview.q: Your quota is 600,000 € a year and your average deal is 20,000 €. What activity do you need?
interview.a: 30 deals. With a 25 % win rate that is 120 opportunities; if 40 % of first meetings become opportunities, 300 first meetings, about 6 or 7 a week over 46 weeks. Then I would check my real conversion rates after the first months and adjust, and look for the lever with the biggest effect, such as a better win rate or larger deals.

interview.q: A big deal you committed is slipping in the last weeks of the quarter. What do you do?
interview.a: Tell my manager immediately with the facts and what is missing, move it out of commit if it no longer meets the criteria, and test it with the buyer: meeting with the economic buyer, mutual close plan with dates. If it really slips, I update the close date and work other deals to close the gap. I would not offer an unrequested discount to force it.

interview.q: How would you grow a key account?
interview.a: Start from the customer’s goals and prove the value already delivered, in QBRs with numbers. Map the relationships and get out of single-threading, especially with the economic buyer. Use a whitespace grid of business units and products to find the next logical project, and agree an account plan with objectives, owners and dates. Expansion follows results; it is not pushed.

interview.q: What is net revenue retention and why does it matter?
interview.a: NRR is starting recurring revenue plus expansion minus contraction and churn, divided by the starting revenue, over a period, usually 12 months. Above 100 % means the existing base grows on its own. It matters because it shows whether customers get value and whether the sales were good sales; gross retention, without expansion, shows the leak.

interview.q: How do you prevent churn in your accounts?
interview.a: A clean handoff to customer success with the promises and success criteria, regular QBRs, and watching warning signs: usage dropping, the champion leaving, a reorganisation, escalations, nobody attending reviews. I start renewal conversations early, often three to four months ahead for large contracts, and keep several relationships in each account so one departure does not put the contract at risk.
